title: Advanced Workflow Threat Modeling
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of advanced workflow threat modeling and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to advanced workflow threat modeling.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on advanced workflow threat modeling. Threat modeling maps trust boundaries, attacker-controlled events, credentials, caches, artifacts, runner state, and which components can influence a privileged deployment. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Advanced Workflow Threat Modeling matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Threat modeling maps trust boundaries, attacker-controlled events, credentials, caches, artifacts, runner state, and which components can influence a privileged deployment. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Threat modeling maps trust boundaries, attacker-controlled events, credentials, caches, artifacts, runner state, and which components can influence a privileged deployment. Optional specializations extend the core workflow model; keep new scanners, docs publishing, container delivery, and release controls scoped, observable, and reviewed. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Threat modeling for workflow triggers
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Trust boundaries between jobs
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Untrusted input analysis
items.text: For untrusted input analysis, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Compromised action scenarios
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Runner isolation strategies
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

items.title: Security incident response
items.text: For security incident response, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

name: Controlled workflow review
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Review permissions, triggers, artifacts, and recovery evidence"

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to advanced workflow threat modeling. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain advanced workflow threat modeling, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Apply optional security, documentation, container, and release specializations after core concepts are understood.

content.task: Apply advanced workflow threat modeling to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Threat modeling maps trust boundaries, attacker-controlled events, credentials, caches, artifacts, runner state, and which components can influence a privileged deployment.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Threat modeling maps trust boundaries, attacker-controlled events, credentials, caches, artifacts, runner state, and which components can influence a privileged deployment. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
